extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and working adults considering an online certificate in novel writing
extracted.subtask_description: Description and evaluation criteria for Stanford University's two-year Online Certificate Program in Novel Writing, including curriculum, pedagogy, application requirements, and student expectations. Useful for prospective applicants assessing fit and program outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program format and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-year certificate program; asynchronous with an optional hour-long Zoom meeting once a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed for busy working adults; participants complete a full-length novel. The program requires one class per term (rather than the typical MFA two-class load), making it suitable for those who cannot take multiple classes simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort model and class size
rubrics_metrics.description: Program accepts 60 students overall; each class includes 15 students who study together with one instructor each term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many students remain with the same cohort for the full two years, workshopping novel chapters together. The small-class/cohort model is presented as fostering camaraderie, mutual support, and a group learning environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly submission expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students typically submit approximately 1,000 words a week over a 10-week course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements differ from instructor to instructor, but the model emphasizes steady weekly writing and regular peer/instructor feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course composition (reading vs. writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each course blends reading, workshopping, and writing; roughly one-quarter of the course is reading and three-quarters is devoted to writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors use published examples to examine how novels are written; reading is explicitly tied to craft lessons and used to inform students' writing and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core curriculum and sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Students take five core courses in sequence during the certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course topics include novel forms and theories (first year), novel plot and structure, theme/language/subtext (following year), and a course focusing on manuscript completion; students must also take one elective (e.g., memoir, poetry, specific fiction genres, or craft elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical approach: workshop + published exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors blend instruction, workshopping, and close study of published opening chapters and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classes look at how beginnings hook readers and whether/where an inciting incident should occur. The approach emphasizes using great published examples to teach novel-writing craft, with a majority of time devoted to writing and responding to peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-on-One Tutorial (post-manuscript option)
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing their manuscript, students may opt for a One-on-One Tutorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are matched with an instructor in a similar genre who reads the entire novel, makes line edits and developmental suggestions, and then guides the student through an immersive term of intense revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application materials and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must submit a writing sample of at least 3,000 words and a paragraph of constructive feedback for revision on the first page of a novel (supplied on the application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must also explain their goals for the program and submit a description of themselves as a person and student and as a potential cohort member. The application evaluates both writing and the applicant's capacity for constructive peer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student prerequisites and readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Program is aimed at working adults who have taken writing classes and have a basic understanding of novel structure and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants do not need a perfectly formed novel outline, but should be ready to commit to a manuscript and willing to put in significant work—the program is pitched as rewarding those who actively engage and contribute to the cohort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors are published and accomplished novelists and current or former Wallace Stegner Fellows; program lists named instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program emphasizes acclaimed faculty as a quality marker, naming several instructors to illustrate expertise and mentorship available to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants may work in contemporary fiction, mystery, thriller, science fiction, historical fiction, autobiographical fiction, and young adult fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The range of genres indicates the program's applicability to many novel-writing tracks and that instructors/peer groups will cover varied genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goals for openings and inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Students study whether their novel needs an inciting incident and where it should occur; examine opening chapters and how those beginnings hook readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction focuses on ensuring the beginning of a novel raises a question that interests readers enough to keep reading, with weekly study of different published opening chapters as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes and evidence of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants are expected to complete a full-length novel; several alumni have gone on to publish (traditionally, hybrid, or independently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites alumni successes (e.g., a New York Times bestseller and other agented/sold debuts) as evidence of the program's effectiveness in preparing writers for publication.
